growth_story.headline: Austria's income per person is back where it was in 2018: an energy shock and two years of recession came on top of a long, slow fade in growth.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Austria's income per person has grown 1.2 percent a year on average, with no lasting break in the trend, but the pace has faded: 0.7 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 0.5 percent over 2016–2025. Growth in the mid-2000s leaned on exports to Central and Eastern Europe, and the collapse in world trade and investment cut income per person by 3.8 percent in 2009. Growth then stalled in 2012–2014 as the euro area crisis and a weak recovery to the east spilled over, and the IMF judged that underlying growth had slowed even before 2008. The pandemic cut income per person by 6.7 percent in 2020, and rebounds of 4.5 and 4.3 percent took it to a peak in 2022. The 2022 energy price shock, Germany's slump and higher interest rates then brought falls of 1.8 percent in 2023 and 1.2 percent in 2024, which the OECD calls the longest recession since 1945. Income per person grew 0.3 percent in 2025 but is still 2.6 percent below its 2022 peak, about where it first was in 2018.

threads.title: Energy shock and long recession
threads.text: Russia's war in Ukraine sent energy prices up from 2022. Together with Germany's slump and higher interest rates, this tipped Austria into two years of recession, its longest since 1945, and the OECD expects a lasting loss in the level of output.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Austria 2026
citations.quote: The downturn, driven by the 2022 energy price shock, hit Austria particularly hard and will have permanent effect on the level of output.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Austria 2026
citations.quote: Austria has high levels of well-being, but has experienced recently its longest recession since 1945.

citations.title: Austria: 2026 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Alternate Executive Director for Austria
citations.quote: Then, Russia’s war in Ukraine, Germany’s multi-year slump and monetary tightening tipped the economy into a 2-year recession

threads.title: Energy and labour costs rise
threads.text: Industry lost ground as energy prices and wages rose, and energy-hungry sectors were hit hardest. Wages in Austria are more widely linked to past inflation than elsewhere in the euro area, and the IMF sees this as the main reason Austria lost competitiveness against the rest of the euro area.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Austria 2026
citations.quote: Business dynamism has declined over the past decade and competitiveness has been eroded by high energy prices and rising labour costs.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Austria 2026
citations.quote: The decline is largely attributable to energy-intensive sectors, which were particularly affected by the rise in energy prices

citations.title: Austria: 2026 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Alternate Executive Director for Austria
citations.quote: Austria has lost competitiveness relative to the Euro area primarily because of the more widespread indexation of wages to past inflation.

threads.title: Slow productivity, ageing workforce
threads.text: Output per worker has grown slowly for years, held back by little capital per worker and more part-time work. The population is ageing, and both the IMF and the OECD expect the workforce to shrink.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Austria 2026
citations.quote: Trend labour productivity growth is low, held back by low capital intensity and rising part-time employment.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Austria 2026
citations.quote: The population is ageing and the labour force will decline.

citations.title: Austria: 2026 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Alternate Executive Director for Austria
citations.quote: reflecting persistently weak labor productivity growth and a shrinking workforce

threads.title: Eastern exports and the crisis
threads.text: In 2005–2007 growth leaned on exports to Central and Eastern Europe. The 2009 collapse in world trade and investment ended that run, and spillovers from the euro area crisis and a weak recovery to the east kept growth close to zero in 2012–2014.

threads.title: An earlier slowdown and immigration
threads.text: The IMF found that underlying growth had begun to slow before the 2008 crisis, as capital built up more slowly, labour input fell and productivity stopped rising. From 2011 more immigrants arrived, as Austria's labour market opened to workers from the newer EU members.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes 2025 as the year Austria emerged from recession, yet income per person rose only 0.3 percent that year and is still 2.6 percent below its 2022 peak. The gap suggests a population that keeps growing, so a recovery in total output shows up only faintly per person.
